claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential directly powers ATP production, mitochondrial protein import, and metabolite transport.
source: Mitochondrial membrane potential directly powers many critical functions of mitochondria, including ATP production, mitochondrial protein import, and metabolite transport.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract about the functions of mitochondrial membrane potential.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial membrane potential is a cardinal feature of aging and mitochondrial diseases.
source: Its loss is a cardinal feature of aging and mitochondrial diseases, and cells closely monitor membrane potential as an indicator of mitochondrial health.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, supported by citations in the introduction (Hagen et al., 1997; Hughes et al., 2020; Leprat et al., 1990; Mansell et al., 2021; Sastre et al., 1996; Sugrue and Tatton, 2001).

claim: Loss of the Sit4 protein phosphatase in yeast increases mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: We report that loss of the Sit4 protein phosphatase in yeast increases mitochondrial membrane potential, both by inducing the electron transport chain and the phosphate starvation response.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Loss of Sit4 increases mitochondrial membrane potential by inducing the electron transport chain.
source: We report that loss of the Sit4 protein phosphatase in yeast increases mitochondrial membrane potential, both by inducing the electron transport chain and the phosphate starvation response.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data (Figure 2A) and BN-PAGE analysis (Figure 2B) showing increased ETC complex abundance in sit4Δ mutants.

claim: Loss of Sit4 increases mitochondrial membrane potential by inducing the phosphate starvation response.
source: We report that loss of the Sit4 protein phosphatase in yeast increases mitochondrial membrane potential, both by inducing the electron transport chain and the phosphate starvation response.
evidence: This is supported by phosphoproteomics and RNA sequencing data (Figure 3A and B) showing activation of PHO regulon targets in sit4Δ mutants.

claim: Elevated mitochondrial membrane potential in sit4Δ mutants is elicited by phosphate starvation or by abrogation of the Pho85-dependent phosphate sensing pathway.
source: Indeed, a similarly elevated mitochondrial membrane potential is also elicited simply by phosphate starvation or by abrogation of the Pho85-dependent phosphate sensing pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased MMP in phosphate-depleted cells (Figure 3C and D) and in pho85Δ mutants (Figure 5A).

claim: Enhanced membrane potential in phosphate-limited conditions is primarily driven by an unexpected activity of the ADP/ATP carrier.
source: This enhanced membrane potential is primarily driven by an unexpected activity of the ADP/ATP carrier.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that bongkrekic acid (an AAC inhibitor) blocks the MMP increase in phosphate-depleted conditions (Figure 4B and C).

claim: The connection between phosphate limitation and enhancement of mitochondrial membrane potential is observed in primary and immortalized mammalian cells.
source: We also demonstrate that this connection between phosphate limitation and enhancement of mitochondrial membrane potential is observed in primary and immortalized mammalian cells as well as in Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in HEK293T and A375 cells (Figure 6A-C) and primary hepatocytes (Figure 6D).

claim: The connection between phosphate limitation and enhancement of mitochondrial membrane potential is observed in Drosophila.
source: We also demonstrate that this connection between phosphate limitation and enhancement of mitochondrial membrane potential is observed in primary and immortalized mammalian cells as well as in Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased MMP in PFA-treated flies (Figure 6E).

claim: Impaired mitochondrial membrane potential is highly correlated with cellular dysfunction in aging.
source: Therefore, it is not surprising that impaired MMP is highly correlated with cellular dysfunction in aging (Hagen et al., 1997; Hughes et al., 2020; Leprat et al., 1990; Mansell et al., 2021; Sastre et al., 1996; Sugrue and Tatton, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial membrane potential is highly correlated with cellular dysfunction in primary mitochondrial disease.
source: Therefore, it is not surprising that impaired MMP is highly correlated with cellular dysfunction in aging (Hagen et al., 1997; Hughes et al., 2020; Leprat et al., 1990; Mansell et al., 2021; Sastre et al., 1996; Sugrue and Tatton, 2001) and a variety of diseases, including primary mitochondrial disease (Burelle et al., 2015; James et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Impaired mitochondrial membrane potential is highly correlated with cellular dysfunction in heart failure.
source: Therefore, it is not surprising that impaired MMP is highly correlated with cellular dysfunction in aging (Hagen et al., 1997; Hughes et al., 2020; Leprat et al., 1990; Mansell et al., 2021; Sastre et al., 1996; Sugrue and Tatton, 2001) and a variety of diseases, including primary mitochondrial disease (Burelle et al., 2015; James et al., 1996) and heart failure (Cluntun et al., 2021; Sharov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activating an artificial proton pump in C. elegans restores the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential typical of aging and is sufficient to extend lifespan.
source: In the context of aging, activating an artificial proton pump in Caenorhabditis elegans restores the loss of MMP typical of aging and is sufficient to extend lifespan (Berry et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Using an artificial proton pump to ectopically increase mitochondrial membrane potential improves the survival of C. elegans treated with electron transport chain inhibitors.
source: In addition, using the same manipulation to ectopically increase MMP improves the survival of C. elegans treated with electron transport chain (ETC) inhibitors (Berry et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The canonical mechanism to generate mitochondrial membrane potential is by complexes I, III, and IV of the electron transport chain, which pump protons from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space.
source: The canonical mechanism to generate MMP is by complexes I, III, and IV of the ETC, which pump protons from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space (IMS).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mitochondrial bioenergetics.

claim: ATP synthase can run in reverse, hydrolyzing ATP to ADP and using the energy to pump protons to the intermembrane space and augment mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: However, several studies have described an alternative mechanism for the generation of MMP, namely ATP synthase running in reverse—hydrolyzing ATP to ADP and using the energy to pump protons to the IMS and augment the MMP (Junge and Nelson, 2015; Okuno et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential is maintained in complex III-deficient cells through ATP synthase running in reverse.
source: For example, Vasan et al. reported that the MMP is maintained in complex III-deficient cells through this ATP synthase mechanism (Vasan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cancer cells tend to have a higher mitochondrial membrane potential relative to normal cells.
source: For example, relative to normal cells, cancer cells tend to have a higher MMP (Davis et al., 1985; Heerdt et al., 2005; Summerhayes et al., 1982)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells experiencing amino acid starvation have higher mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: For example, relative to normal cells, cancer cells tend to have a higher MMP (Davis et al., 1985; Heerdt et al., 2005; Summerhayes et al., 1982) as do cells experiencing amino acid starvation (Johnson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Oxidative stress decreases mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Generally, nutrient and other biological stress scenarios also modulate MMP (Hübscher et al., 2016, p. 70; Pan et al., 2011); in particular, oxidative stress has been shown to decrease MMP (Korshunov et al., 1997; Satoh et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of the mtFAS pathway results in the absence of the lipoic acid cofactor.
source: We and others showed that loss of this pathway results in the absence of the lipoic acid cofactor as well as loss of acylated acyl carrier protein (ACP), which is required for the assembly and activation of many mitochondrial complexes, including each ETC complex (Angerer et al., 2017; Brody et al., 1997; Nowinski et al., 2020; Van Vranken et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies including the authors' own work.

claim: Loss of the mtFAS pathway results in loss of acylated acyl carrier protein (ACP), which is required for the assembly and activation of many mitochondrial complexes, including each ETC complex.
source: We and others showed that loss of this pathway results in the absence of the lipoic acid cofactor as well as loss of acylated acyl carrier protein (ACP), which is required for the assembly and activation of many mitochondrial complexes, including each ETC complex (Angerer et al., 2017; Brody et al., 1997; Nowinski et al., 2020; Van Vranken et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies including the authors' own work.

claim: The mct1Δ mutant lacks assembly of the electron transport chain.
source: This was surprising given that mct1Δ cells lack assembly of the ETC, the major producer of MMP (Van Vranken et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and confirmed by BN-PAGE data in Figure 2B.

claim: The mct1Δ mutant exhibited a more fragmented mitochondrial morphology.
source: We found that mct1Δ cells exhibited a more fragmented mitochondrial morphology, consistent with previous observations in other respiratory-deficient strains (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: Deletion of SIT4 resulted in more reticular and less fragmented or aggregated mitochondria, both in the presence or absence of the mct1Δ mutation.
source: whereas deletion of SIT4 resulted in more reticular and less fragmented or aggregated mitochondria, both in the presence or absence of the mct1Δ mutation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Deletion of SIT4 caused a complete loss of uncleaved Ilv2-FLAG, suggesting more efficient import into mitochondria.
source: In contrast, deletion of SIT4 caused a complete loss of uncleaved Ilv2-FLAG, whether or not MCT1 was also deleted (Figure 1F and G). We interpret these data as suggesting that Ilv2-FLAG is more efficiently imported into mitochondria in the absence of SIT4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: The sit4Δ mutant exhibited elevated expression of most of the genes encoding subunits of the ETC and ATP synthase.
source: RNA sequencing revealed that the sit4Δ mutant exhibited elevated expression of most of the genes encoding subunits of the ETC and ATP synthase, which could potentially promote ETC complex formation and function (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mitochondria from mct1Δ mutant showed a complete loss of all the ETC complexes.
source: As previously reported, mitochondria from mct1Δ mutant showed a complete loss of all the ETC complexes (Van Vranken et al., 2018; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and confirmed by BN-PAGE data in Figure 2B.

claim: Every ETC complex and supercomplex assembly was enriched in the sit4Δ mutant.
source: Conversely and consistent with the RNA sequencing data, every ETC complex and supercomplex assembly was enriched in the sit4Δ mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion of SIT4 completely reversed the absence of and further enriched the abundance of ETC and ATP synthase complexes in mct1Δ cells.
source: Strikingly, deletion of SIT4 also completely reversed the absence of and further enriched the abundance of ETC and ATP synthase complexes in mct1Δ cells.
evidence: This is supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: mct1Δ sit4Δ cells still lacked acylated ACP, indicating that mtFAS remains inactive upon deletion of SIT4.
source: however, mct1Δ sit4Δ cells still lacked acylated ACP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and lipoic acid as measured by lipoylation of Lat1 and Kgd2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), indicating that mtFAS remains inactive upon deletion of SIT4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The mct1Δ mutant exhibited a profound decrease in oxygen consumption rate.
source: As expected, the mct1Δ mutant exhibited a profound decrease in OCR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: sit4Δ cells exhibited an elevated oxygen consumption rate consistent with their increased abundance of ETC complexes.
source: On the other hand, sit4Δ cells exhibited an elevated OCR consistent with their increased abundance of ETC complexes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mct1Δ sit4Δ cells showed an oxygen consumption rate that was increased relative to the mct1Δ single mutant, but still significantly lower than the wild-type OCR.
source: The mct1Δ sit4Δ cells showed an OCR that was increased relative to the mct1Δ single mutant, but still significantly lower than the wild-type OCR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: sit4Δ cells failed to grow on media containing a non-fermentable carbon source such as glycerol that requires mitochondrial respiration.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Arndt et al., 1989; Dimmer et al., 2002; Jablonka et al., 2006), sit4Δ cells failed to grow on media containing a non-fermentable carbon source such as glycerol that requires mitochondrial respiration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Overexpression of HAP4 was sufficient to increase the abundance of each OXPHOS complex as assessed by BN-PAGE.
source: Overexpression of HAP4, the catalytic component of the HAP complex, was sufficient to increase the abundance of each OXPHOS complex as assessed by BN-PAGE (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HAP4 overexpression failed to rescue the loss of any of the OXPHOS complexes observed in the mct1Δ background.
source: However, HAP4 overexpression failed to rescue the loss of any of the OXPHOS complexes observed in the mct1Δ background (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HAP4 overexpression had no effect on mitochondrial membrane potential in either wild-type or mct1Δ cells.
source: It also had no effect on MMP in either wild-type or mct1Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Loss of HAP4 suppressed, but did not eliminate, the increased mitochondrial membrane potential observed in sit4Δ cells.
source: Loss of HAP4 suppressed, but did not eliminate, the increased MMP observed in sit4Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Deletion of SIT4 was sufficient to increase mitochondrial membrane potential whether or not complex III or IV was inactivated, albeit not to the same extent as in wild-type cells.
source: Whether or not complex III or IV was inactivated, deletion of SIT4 was sufficient to increase MMP, albeit not to the same extent as in wild-type cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Inhibiting the ATP synthase with oligomycin led to an increase of mitochondrial membrane potential in both wild-type and sit4Δ cells.
source: Inhibiting the ATP synthase led to an increase of MMP in both wild-type and sit4Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), suggesting that ATP synthase operates in the direction of MMP consumption and ATP generation in sit4Δ cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The rpo41Δ mutant lacks the proton-pumping ETC complexes III and IV as well as the protein-transducing Fo component of the ATP synthase.
source: As a result, the rpo41Δ mutant lacks the proton-pumping ETC complexes III and IV as well as the protein-transducing Fo component of the ATP synthase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The mitochondrial membrane potential of the rpo41Δ mutant is very low, even significantly lower than that of mct1Δ cells.
source: As expected, the MMP of the rpo41Δ mutant is very low, even significantly lower than that of mct1Δ cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Deletion of SIT4 in the rpo41Δ mutant background restored the mitochondrial membrane potential to a level similar to wild-type cells.
source: However, deletion of SIT4 in the rpo41Δ mutant background restored the MMP to a level similar to wild-type cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Complex II accumulated more assembled complex upon SIT4 deletion in the rpo41Δ mutant.
source: Intriguingly, complex II, which does not contain any mtDNA-encoded subunits, accumulated more assembled complex upon SIT4 deletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Among the most enriched phosphoproteins in sit4Δ mutants, Pho84, Vtc3, and Spl2 are all involved in the regulation of intracellular phosphate levels.
source: Among the most enriched phosphoproteins, Pho84, Vtc3, and Spl2 are all involved in the regulation of intracellular phosphate levels (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Many of the most significant transcriptional increases in the sit4Δ mutant were transcriptional targets of the PHO regulon.
source: In addition, we cross-referenced our phosphoproteomics and RNA sequencing data (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2) and confirmed that many of the most significant transcriptional increases in the sit4Δ mutant were transcriptional targets of the PHO regulon (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Wild-type cells exhibited an increase in mitochondrial membrane potential over an 8 hr time course when grown in low phosphate concentrations (50, 10, or 1 μM), but not in cells grown in either 100 μM or 10 mM phosphate.
source: Over an 8 hr time course, we observed an increase in the MMP of wild-type cells grown in low phosphate concentrations (50, 10, or 1 μM), but not in cells grown in either 100 μM or 10 mM phosphate (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: rho0 cells exhibited elevated mitochondrial membrane potential in response to phosphate depletion (1 μM Pi), although the response was delayed compared to wild-type cells.
source: Indeed, rho0 cells exhibited elevated MMP in response to phosphate depletion (1 μM Pi), although the response was delayed compared to wild-type cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mitochondrial protein import, as measured by Ilv2-FLAG cleavage, was enhanced by phosphate depletion in wild-type cells.
source: Consistent with the MMP increase, mitochondrial protein import, as measured by Ilv2-FLAG cleavage, was enhanced by phosphate depletion in wild-type cells (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: rho0 cells have a significant import deficiency, but this defect was mostly rescued by phosphate depletion.
source: rho0 cells have a significant import deficiency, but this defect was mostly rescued by phosphate depletion as well (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: In wild-type cells, phosphate depletion led to a modest enrichment in ETC complex abundance compared to cells grown in normal phosphate concentrations.
source: Using BN-PAGE, we found that in wild-type cells, phosphate depletion led to a modest enrichment in ETC complex abundance compared to cells grown in normal phosphate concentrations (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Depleting phosphate in rho0 cells failed to rescue the absence of the ETC complexes.
source: Inversely, as expected, depleting phosphate in rho0 cells failed to rescue the absence of the complexes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Phosphate depletion led to an accumulation in assembled complex II in rho0 cells.
source: Similar to the complex II enrichment in rpo41Δ sit4Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I), phosphate depletion also led to an accumulation in assembled complex II in rho0 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Most of the membrane potential was lost in cells treated with antimycin A in either normal or low phosphate-containing media.
source: Most of the membrane potential was lost in cells treated with antimycin A in either normal or low phosphate-containing media (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Even in the presence of antimycin A, low phosphate still triggered a similarly fold elevation in membrane potential.
source: however, even in the presence of antimycin A, low phosphate still triggered a similarly fold elevation in membrane potential.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Treatment of wild-type cells with bongkrekic acid significantly dampened the phosphate depletion-mediated increase in mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Treatment of wild-type cells with bongkrekic acid significantly dampened the phosphate depletion-mediated increase in MMP (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Combination treatment with both antimycin A and bongkrekic acid completely blocked the induction of mitochondrial membrane potential in response to low phosphate.
source: Importantly, combination treatment with both antimycin A and bongkrekic acid completely blocked the induction of MMP in response to low phosphate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Phosphate depletion triggers an enhanced mitochondrial membrane potential in rho0 cells, but this is completely eliminated by bongkrekic acid in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As shown before, phosphate depletion triggers an enhanced MMP in rho0 cells, but this is completely eliminated by bongkrekic acid in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Deletion of PHO85 in yeast cells results in constitutive activation of the PHO regulon even in a high phosphate environment.
source: Deletion of PHO85 in yeast cells results in constitutive activation of the PHO regulon even in a high phosphate environment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the phosphate signaling pathway in yeast.

claim: pho85Δ cells accumulate twice as much phosphate as wild-type cells.
source: As a result, pho85Δ cells accumulate twice as much phosphate as wild-type cells (Gupta et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential was significantly increased in pho85Δ cells.
source: To elucidate how environmental phosphate starvation induces high MMP, we measured the MMP in pho85Δ mutants and found that, similar to sit4Δ cells or cells grown in phosphate-depleted media, MMP was significantly increased in pho85Δ cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: In the context of MCT1 deletion, the pho85Δ also increased mitochondrial membrane potential, restoring the mct1Δ to near wild-type membrane potential.
source: In the context of MCT1 deletion, the pho85Δ also increased MMP, restoring the mct1Δ to near wild-type membrane potential (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The pho85Δ mutant shared a similar distribution of reticular, fragment/aggregated, or mixed mitochondrial morphology with wild-type cells.
source: In spite of having an elevated MMP, the pho85Δ mutant shared a similar distribution of reticular, fragment/aggregated, or mixed mitochondrial morphology with wild-type cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PHO85 deletion normalized the fragmented and aggregated mitochondrial phenotype of mct1Δ cells.
source: However, PHO85 deletion normalized the fragmented and aggregated mitochondrial phenotype of mct1Δ cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The pho85Δ mutant had improved import of Ilv2-FLAG than wild-type cells.
source: We also confirmed the MMP observation by demonstrating that the pho85Δ mutant had improved import of Ilv2-FLAG than wild-type cells, and PHO85 deletion restored the import activity of the mct1Δ mutant to around wild-type levels (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: PHO85 deletion restored the import activity of the mct1Δ mutant to around wild-type levels.
source: We also confirmed the MMP observation by demonstrating that the pho85Δ mutant had improved import of Ilv2-FLAG than wild-type cells, and PHO85 deletion restored the import activity of the mct1Δ mutant to around wild-type levels (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: There was a modest enrichment of ETC complexes in the pho85Δ mutant.
source: Consistent with phosphate-depleted wild-type cells as shown in Figure 4A, there was a modest enrichment of ETC complexes in the pho85Δ mutant (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In the context of the mct1Δ mutant strain, deletion of PHO85 had no effect on the complete loss of ETC complexes.
source: In the context of the mct1Δ mutant strain, however, deletion of PHO85 had no effect on the complete loss of ETC complexes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: pho85Δ cells exhibit no increase in the abundance of mRNAs encoding ETC and ATP synthase subunits.
source: We reasoned that this lack of rescue was different from SIT4 deletion because pho85Δ cells exhibit no increase in the abundance of mRNAs encoding ETC and ATP synthase subunits (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, compared to Figure 2A for sit4Δ, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Deleting PHO85 partially rescued the lethality of the atp1Δ mct1Δ and atp2Δ mct1Δ double mutants.
source: However, deleting PHO85 partially rescued the lethality of the double mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Both HEK293T and A375 cells exhibited increased mitochondrial membrane potential after 3 d of growth in phosphate-free medium.
source: Both HEK293T and A375 cells exhibited increased MMP after 3 d of growth in phosphate-free medium (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HEK293T and A375 cells grown in low phosphate exhibited a more connected and elongated mitochondrial network.
source: Consistent with the increased MMP, HEK293T and A375 cells grown in low phosphate exhibited a more connected and elongated mitochondrial network (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment with the phosphate transporter inhibitor phosphonoformic acid (PFA) for 48 hr resulted in a dose-dependent increase in mitochondrial membrane potential in HEK293T and A375 cells.
source: As an alternative strategy to limit phosphate uptake from the media, we treated these same cell lines with the phosphate transporter inhibitor phosphonoformic acid (PFA) for 48 hr. We observed a dose-dependent increase in MMP in both cell lines (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Primary hepatocytes treated with PFA for 24 hr showed a dose-dependent increase in mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Similar to the immortalized cell lines, MMP increased in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PFA-treated adult flies exhibited a higher mitochondrial membrane potential than the control group as measured by quantification of TMRE-stained images of the fly midgut.
source: Indeed, PFA-treated adult flies exhibited a higher MMP than the control group as measured by quantification of TMRE-stained images of the fly midgut (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Older flies exhibited more Smurf dye uptake, indicative of more leakiness of the gut epithelium.
source: Older flies exhibited more Smurf dye uptake, indicative of more leakiness of the gut epithelium (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: PFA treatment in either young or old flies improved gut integrity.
source: PFA treatment in either young or old flies improved gut integrity (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Older flies demonstrated a delayed response in negative geotaxis assay, which was rescued by PFA treatment.
source: We also performed a negative geotaxis assay (Gargano et al., 2005), wherein older flies demonstrated a delayed response, which was rescued by PFA treatment (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G and a citation to the method.

claim: PFA treatment increased the maximum lifespan of wild-type flies, but did not affect the average lifespan.
source: PFA treatment increased the maximum lifespan of wild-type flies, but did not affect the average lifespan (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A previous study showed that deletion of SIT4 in rho- cells reverses some of the defects associated with mtDNA damage.
source: Additionally, a previous study by Garipler et al. showed that deletion of SIT4 in rho- cells, where the majority of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is depleted, reverses some of the defects associated with mtDNA damage (Garipler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Deletion of MCT1 does not become rho- as shown by hybrid complementation assays.
source: Despite their shared mitochondrial dysfunction, deletion of MCT1 does not become rho- as shown by hybrid complementation assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The increased mitochondrial membrane potential observed in sit4Δ mutants was also maintained in mct1Δ sit4Δ double mutants.
source: The increased MMP observed in sit4Δ mutants was also maintained in mct1Δ sit4Δ double mutants (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The mct1Δ sit4Δ double mutant exhibited a modest increase in mitochondrial area.
source: The mct1Δ sit4Δ double mutant also exhibited a modest increase in mitochondrial area (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: sit4Δ cells treated with 75 μM CCCP have a mitochondrial membrane potential that is comparable to wild-type cells.
source: We found that sit4Δ cells treated with 75 μM CCCP have an MMP that is comparable to wild-type cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: sit4Δ cells treated with 75 μM CCCP exhibited a similar level of unimported Ilv2-FLAG as wild-type.
source: These cells exhibited a similar level of unimported Ilv2-FLAG as wild-type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and J.

claim: The canonical mitochondrial biogenesis transcriptional response was almost completely absent in the mct1Δ cells, as evidenced by the lack of induction of mRNAs encoding subunits of the ETC and ATP synthase.
source: The canonical mitochondrial biogenesis transcriptional response was almost completely absent in the mct1Δ cells, as evidenced by the lack of induction of mRNAs encoding subunits of the ETC and ATP synthase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mct1Δ mutant increased mRNA abundance of genes encoding proteins primarily related to mechanisms for acetyl-CoA production—a gene response signature that was not exhibited in wild-type cells.
source: Instead, the mct1Δ mutant increased mRNA abundance of genes encoding proteins primarily related to mechanisms for acetyl-CoA production—a gene response signature that was not exhibited in wild-type cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Deletion of SIT4 not only attenuated induction of CIT2, DLD3, ADH2, and CAT2, but also induced the expression of several genes encoding ETC subunits, including QCR2 and RIP1, that were repressed in the mct1Δ mutant.
source: Second, deletion of SIT4 not only attenuated induction of these four genes, but also induced the expression of several genes encoding ETC subunits, including QCR2 and RIP1, that were repressed in the mct1Δ mutant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of SIT4 alone—without a concomitant loss of MCT1—alters the abundance of CIT2, DLD3, ADH2, CAT2, QCR2, and RIP1 mRNAs tested, indicating that this transcriptional effect of SIT4 deletion is independent of the underlying mitochondrial defects.
source: Notably, deletion of SIT4 alone—without a concomitant loss of MCT1—alters the abundance of these mRNAs tested, indicating that this transcriptional effect of SIT4 deletion is independent of the underlying mitochondrial defects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The increased mitochondrial membrane potential in sit4Δ mutants cannot be explained by glucose de-repression.
source: This result indicates that the increased MMP caused by SIT4 deletion cannot be explained by glucose de-repression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C comparing MMP in glucose vs raffinose media.

claim: The modest increase in oxygen consumption in mct1Δ sit4Δ double mutant is insufficient to explain the profound increase in mitochondrial membrane potential observed relative to the mct1Δ single mutant.
source: Moreover, the observed modest increase in oxygen consumption is insufficient to explain the profound increase in MMP observed in the mct1Δ sit4Δ double mutant relative to the mct1Δ single mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of OCR data (Figure 2C) and MMP data (Figure 1D).

claim: sit4Δ cells partially require the Hap complex to generate higher mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Therefore, we concluded that sit4Δ cells partially require the Hap complex to generate higher MMP, but overexpressing HAP4 is insufficient to increase MMP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that loss of HAP4 suppresses but does not eliminate increased MMP in sit4Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).

claim: Overexpressing HAP4 is insufficient to increase mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Therefore, we concluded that sit4Δ cells partially require the Hap complex to generate higher MMP, but overexpressing HAP4 is insufficient to increase MMP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing HAP4 overexpression had no effect on MMP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Although ETC activity is required for the majority of the enhanced mitochondrial membrane potential observed in sit4Δ cells, sit4Δ mutants clearly leverage additional ETC- and ATP synthase-independent mechanisms to increase mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: These results demonstrated that although ETC activity is required for the majority of the enhanced MMP observed in sit4Δ cells, sit4Δ mutants clearly leverage additional ETC- and ATP synthase-independent mechanisms to increase mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased MMP in sit4Δ rpo41Δ cells (Figure 2E) and the schematic in Figure 2F.

claim: Phosphate deprivation does not induce massive changes in mitochondrial morphology in wild-type cells.
source: Finally, the quantification of mitochondrial morphology suggested that phosphate deprivation does not induce massive changes in mitochondrial morphology in wild-type cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The fragmented and aggregated mitochondria in rho0 cells was partially rescued by phosphate depletion.
source: However, the fragmented and aggregated mitochondria in rho0 cells was partially rescued by phosphate depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ETC complexes are slightly enriched with phosphate depletion, but this is not required for the increase in mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Together with the BN-PAGE results, we concluded that ETC complexes are slightly enriched with phosphate depletion, but this is not required for the increase in MMP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing modest ETC enrichment (Figure 4A) but MMP increase even with antimycin A treatment (Figure 4B).

claim: When cells lack the proton-pumping ability of the ETC and particularly during phosphate depletion, they rely on the ADP/ATP carrier to increase mitochondrial membrane potential to sustain critical mitochondrial functions.
source: Our data suggest that when cells lack the proton-pumping ability of the ETC—either by chemical treatment (i.e., antimycin A) or genetic inhibition (mtDNA loss in rho0 cells)—and particularly during phosphate depletion, they instead rely on the ADP/ATP carrier to increase MMP to sustain critical mitochondrial functions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that bongkrekic acid blocks MMP increase in phosphate-depleted rho0 cells (Figure 4C).

claim: The mechanism underlying the MMP increase in response to phosphate starvation is unlikely to be a direct result of intracellular phosphate insufficiency.
source: These phenotypes of the pho85Δ mutant strain suggest that the mechanism underlying the MMP increase in response to phosphate starvation is unlikely to be a direct result of intracellular phosphate insufficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that pho85Δ cells have elevated intracellular phosphate but still show increased MMP.

claim: The perception of phosphate starvation, and activation of the phosphate signaling response, is the key driver of mitochondrial membrane potential enhancement.
source: Rather, these data support the hypothesis that the perception of phosphate starvation, and activation of the phosphate signaling response, is the key driver of MMP enhancement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that pho85Δ cells (which have high intracellular phosphate but active PHO signaling) show increased MMP.

claim: Activating phosphate starvation signaling is sufficient to establish an elevated mitochondrial membrane potential, in a manner that is mostly independent of the ETC.
source: We therefore concluded that activating phosphate starvation signaling is sufficient to establish an elevated MMP, in a manner that is mostly independent of the ETC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that pho85Δ does not rescue ETC complexes in mct1Δ background but still increases MMP (Figure 5E and 5A).

claim: mct1Δ pho85Δ cells exhibit a much higher mitochondrial membrane potential compared to the mct1Δ mutant, and this appears to largely be mediated by ETC- and ATP synthase-independent mechanisms.
source: In particular, mct1Δ pho85Δ cells exhibit a much higher MMP compared to the mct1Δ mutant, and this appears to largely be mediated by ETC- and ATP synthase-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased MMP in mct1Δ pho85Δ cells (Figure 5A) despite no rescue of ETC complexes (Figure 5E).

claim: Deleting PHO85 partially rescued the lethality of atp1Δ mct1Δ and atp2Δ mct1Δ double mutants, suggesting that additional ATPase(s) beyond the F1 subunit of ATP synthase couple with ADP/ATP carrier activity to generate mitochondrial membrane potential in the phosphate-depleted condition.
source: However, deleting PHO85 partially rescued the lethality of the double mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G). These data suggest that additional ATPase(s) beyond the F1 subunit of ATP synthase couple with ADP/ATP carrier activity to generate MMP in the phosphate-depleted condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic rescue data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Phosphate depletion induces a higher mitochondrial membrane potential in cultured mammalian cell lines.
source: We concluded that phosphate depletion induces a higher MMP in cultured mammalian cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in HEK293T and A375 cells (Figure 6A-C).

claim: Phosphate limitation can extend lifespan in yeast, flies, and mice.
source: It has been well established that phosphate limitation can extend lifespan in yeast, flies, and mice (Bergwitz et al., 2013; Ebrahimi et al., 2021; Kurosu et al., 2005; Kurosu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Excessive phosphate shortens lifespan in flies and mice.
source: In both the fly and mouse, it was also conversely demonstrated that excessive phosphate shortens lifespan (Bergwitz et al., 2013; Kuro-o et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PFA treatment extends lifespan in flies.
source: From the evidence presented herein (Figure 6E–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), as well as the previous study showing that PFA treatment extends lifespan (Bergwitz et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PFA treatment enhances intestinal health in flies.
source: From the evidence presented herein (Figure 6E–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), as well as the previous study showing that PFA treatment extends lifespan (Bergwitz et al., 2013) and enhances intestinal health in flies (Xu et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Phosphate deprivation increased mitochondrial membrane potential and overall mitochondrial health, thereby enabling lifespan extension.
source: we hypothesize that phosphate deprivation increased MMP and overall mitochondrial health, and thereby enabled lifespan extension.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the authors' data and previous studies.

claim: Boosting mitochondrial membrane potential by photo-activation of an ectopically expressed proton pump is sufficient to prolong lifespan in C. elegans.
source: This connection is supported by a recent study that demonstrated that boosting MMP by photo-activation of an ectopically expressed proton pump is sufficient to prolong lifespan in C. elegans (Berry et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cells establish and maintain a mitochondrial membrane potential 'setpoint', which is tailored to maintain optimal mitochondrial function based on energetic demand, environmental status, and intracellular signaling.
source: As a result, we propose a putative model that, based on energetic demand, environmental status, and intracellular signaling, cells establish and maintain a MMP 'setpoint', which is tailored to maintain optimal mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Cells deploy multiple ETC-dependent and -independent strategies to maintain the mitochondrial membrane potential setpoint.
source: We find that cells deploy multiple ETC-dependent and -independent strategies to maintain that setpoint.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' data showing both ETC-dependent (Figure 2) and ETC-independent (Figure 4) mechanisms.

claim: Cells often prioritize the mitochondrial membrane potential setpoint over other bioenergetic priorities, even in challenging environments.
source: Critically, we find that cells often prioritize this MMP setpoint over other bioenergetic priorities, even in challenging environments, suggesting an important evolutionary benefit.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations that cells use ATP hydrolysis to maintain MMP even when ATP is scarce.

claim: SIT4 is a serine/threonine phosphatase related to human PP6 that plays important roles in cell cycle regulation, TOR signaling, and tRNA modification.
source: SIT4 is a serine/threonine phosphatase related to human PP6 that plays important roles in cell cycle regulation (Clotet et al., 1999; Fernandez-Sarabia et al., 1992; Sutton et al., 1991), TOR signaling (Rohde et al., 2004; Torres et al., 2002), and tRNA modification (Abdel-Fattah et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The PHO regulon stimulates phosphate acquisition triggered by either phosphate depletion or by dysregulation of the phosphate signaling pathway.
source: which stimulates phosphate acquisition triggered by either phosphate depletion or by dysregulation of the phosphate signaling pathway (Oshima, 1997; Paolo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When the ADP/ATP carrier imports ATP4- and exports ADP3-, a net export of a positive charge occurs out of the matrix to the IMS.
source: When the ADP/ATP carrier imports ATP4- and exports ADP3-, a net export of a positive charge occurs out of the matrix to the IMS (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the mechanism of the ADP/ATP carrier.

claim: The activity of the ADP/ATP carrier must be coupled to ATP hydrolysis within the mitochondrial matrix.
source: This activity must be coupled to ATP hydrolysis within the mitochondrial matrix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of how the ADP/ATP carrier generates MMP.

claim: The activity of the ADP/ATP carrier would be coupled to the export of phosphate from the matrix, which is co-transported with a proton through the phosphate carrier.
source: It would also be coupled to the export of phosphate from the matrix, which is co-transported with a proton through the phosphate carrier.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of phosphate transport.

claim: The mitochondrial ATP hydrolysis pathway enables the liberation of needed phosphate from ATP while capturing the released energy in the form of mitochondrial membrane potential rather than having it be simply lost as heat.
source: We propose a speculative hypothesis that this mechanism enables the liberation of needed phosphate from the most abundant labile store of phosphate, ATP. However, cleaving the phosphodiester bonds of ATP releases energy in addition to releasing phosphate. Using this mitochondrial mechanism enables the cell to capture that energy in the form of the MMP rather than having it be simply lost as heat.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The elevated mitochondrial membrane potential enables the cell to better combat nutrient scarcity.
source: As a result, the elevated MMP is able to fuel mitochondrial processes and empowers the cell to better combat nutrient scarcity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the authors' model.
